stem: A teammate wants to run Claude Code from a shell script so that it answers one prompt, prints the response and exits. Which flag turns on that non-interactive mode?

options.text: `-p` (long form `--print`)
options.why: `-p` runs the prompt without the terminal UI, prints the result to stdout and exits, which is what scripts and CI need.

options.text: `--bg`, which starts the session in the background
options.why: `--bg` starts a background session and returns an id for `claude attach`. Claude Code rejects it in combination with `-p`.

options.text: `--bare`, the minimal startup mode recommended for scripts
options.why: `--bare` skips auto-discovery of hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md. It is recommended alongside `-p`, but on its own it does not make the session non-interactive.

options.text: `--verbose`, for full turn-by-turn output
options.why: `--verbose` shows full turn-by-turn output. It does not change whether the session is interactive.

explanation: `claude -p "prompt"` is headless mode: the same agent loop and tools, no terminal UI, output on stdout, and an exit code scripts can branch on (0 on success, non-zero when the run fails). Many automation flags, such as `--output-format`, `--max-turns`, `--json-schema` and `--max-budget-usd`, only work together with `-p`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically

stem: In `claude -p`, what is the default value of `--output-format` when you do not pass the flag? Type the value.
explanation: The three values are `text` (the default: just Claude's answer), `json` (one result object at the end, with the answer in `result` plus the session ID, usage and cost) and `stream-json` (newline-delimited JSON events as the run progresses, ending with a `result` line).
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Get structured output)

stem: A bash script runs `claude -p` once and then needs both the conversation's session ID and its estimated cost, read from a single JSON object with `jq`. Which output format fits?

options.text: `--output-format json`, then read `.session_id` and `.total_cost_usd`
options.why: `json` prints one result object with the answer in `result` plus the session ID, usage and `total_cost_usd`.

options.text: `--output-format text`, then grep the last line of stdout for the session ID
options.why: Text output is only Claude's answer. It carries no session metadata to grep for.

options.text: `--output-format stream-json`, then parse just the first line, the `system/init` event
options.why: The init event has the session ID but not the cost, which arrives on the last line in the `result` message. The stream is also many objects, not one.

options.text: `--json-schema` with a schema that declares `session_id` and `cost` properties
options.why: A schema shapes Claude's own answer. Claude cannot reliably know its session ID or spend, and the real values already sit in the `json` envelope.

explanation: Pick `json` when a script wants one parseable object after the run, and `stream-json` when it needs events as they happen. With `--continue` or `--resume`, `total_cost_usd` reports the whole conversation's total, earlier runs included, and it is a client-side estimate rather than your bill.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Get structured output)

stem: `claude -p` reads standard input, so `cat build-error.txt | claude -p 'explain the root cause'` sends the log to Claude together with the prompt.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: headless mode reads piped stdin, so Claude Code works like any other filter in a shell pipeline.

options.text: False
options.why: Piping is a documented pattern. You do not need to pass a file path or grant a Read permission for piped content.

explanation: Piped stdin is capped at 10 MB; above that Claude Code exits with an error and a non-zero status, so write large inputs to a file and name the path in the prompt instead. Piping has a permission benefit too: `git diff main | claude -p ...` means Claude does not need Bash permission to read the diff.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Pipe data through Claude)

stem: A CI script starts several `claude -p` reviews in parallel in the same directory and later sends a follow-up to one specific review. What is the reliable way to target that review?

options.text: Capture `session_id` from its JSON output and pass it to `claude -p --resume "$id"`
options.why: A session ID names exactly one conversation, whichever order the parallel runs finished in.

options.text: Run `claude -p --continue`, which picks up the most recent conversation in the directory
options.why: With parallel runs, the most recent conversation is whichever finished last, not necessarily the review you want.

options.text: Add `--fork-session` to the follow-up so Claude Code finds the matching review
options.why: `--fork-session` only matters together with `--resume` or `--continue`, where it gives the resumed copy a new ID. It does not choose a session.

options.text: Re-send the original prompt with the follow-up appended; Claude Code merges it into the same session
options.why: Every `-p` run without `--resume` or `--continue` starts a fresh conversation. Nothing is merged.

explanation: `--continue` is convenient for a single sequential script; `--resume <id>` is the safe choice once runs overlap. Claude Code finds a session by ID in any project on the machine, and `--resume` also accepts the absolute path of a session's `.jsonl` transcript file.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Continue conversations)

stem: Match each need in a scripted run with the `claude -p` flag that meets it.

options.text: `--max-turns`
options.why: Caps agentic turns; the run exits with an error at the limit.

options.text: `--max-budget-usd`
options.why: Stops the run once estimated spend reaches the amount.

options.text: `--json-schema`
options.why: Validates the final answer against a JSON Schema and returns it in `structured_output`.

options.text: `--no-session-persistence`
options.why: Keeps the session off disk, so it cannot be resumed.

prompts.text: Stop a runaway agent after a fixed number of tool-use round trips
Keep a nightly job's spend under a dollar figure
Hand a downstream parser an object with a known shape
Run an ephemeral job whose transcript must never be written to the runner's disk

explanation: All four flags are print-mode only. `--max-turns` has no limit by default. `--max-budget-usd` is checked against Claude Code's client-side cost estimate, so leave headroom. `--json-schema` is normally paired with `--output-format json`. `--no-session-persistence` means a later `--resume` cannot find the session.
reference: Claude Code docs: CLI reference (CLI flags)

stem: In a workflow that uses `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`, you want to pass `--max-turns 5` and `--model` to Claude Code. Where do they go?

options.text: In the `claude_args` input, written as CLI arguments
options.why: `claude_args` accepts any Claude Code CLI argument, such as `--max-turns`, `--model`, `--mcp-config` and `--allowedTools`.

options.text: In separate `max_turns` and `model` inputs under `with:`
options.why: Those are beta-era inputs. Upgrading to v1 moves CLI options such as these into `claude_args`.

options.text: In the `prompt` input, as a sentence telling Claude its limits
options.why: The prompt is Claude's instructions. A turn limit written there is advice, not an enforced cap, and it cannot pick the model.

options.text: In a generic `args` input, which GitHub passes to every action
options.why: An action only receives the inputs it declares. This action's input for CLI flags is `claude_args`.

explanation: A typical line is `claude_args: "--max-turns 5 --model <model> --allowedTools ..."`. Other common inputs are `prompt` (automation mode), `anthropic_api_key` or `claude_code_oauth_token` for auth, and `settings` for Claude Code settings JSON.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions (Pass CLI arguments)

stem: Your platform is written in Go. You want the same agent loop, tools and context management that Claude Code uses, without adding a Python or TypeScript service. What does the Agent SDK documentation recommend?

options.text: Run the `claude` CLI as a subprocess with `-p` and `--output-format json`, and parse its output
options.why: This is the documented way to drive the agent loop from a language that has no SDK package.

options.text: Call the Messages API and declare tools named `Bash`, `Read` and `Edit` so the API runs them for you
options.why: Tools you declare on the Messages API are client tools that your own code must execute. Matching Claude Code's names does not give you its implementations.

options.text: Start `claude` interactively inside a pseudo-terminal and scrape the rendered screen
options.why: Fragile, and unnecessary: headless mode exists to give machine-readable output.

options.text: Launch `claude --bg` and read the answer afterwards with `claude logs`
options.why: `claude logs` prints a background session's recent terminal output for people to read. It is not a structured result.

explanation: The CLI is the Agent SDK's runtime, and `claude -p` exposes it to any language: JSON or stream-JSON on stdout, an exit code, and flags for tools, permissions, budgets and sessions. Use `stream-json` when the Go side needs events while the run is in progress.
reference: Agent SDK docs: Agent SDK overview

stem: A script needs Claude's answer as an object shaped `{"functions": [string]}`, validated against a schema. Which invocation is correct?

options.text: `claude -p "..." --output-format json --json-schema '<schema>'`, then read `.structured_output`
options.why: This is the documented pair of flags. The validated object arrives in `structured_output`, next to the session metadata.

options.text: `claude -p "..." --output-format json`, then run `jq '.result | fromjson'` on the output
options.why: `result` holds the text answer. Even if the prompt asks for JSON, nothing validates it, so `fromjson` breaks on prose or a code fence.

options.text: `claude -p "..." --output-format stream-json --json-schema '<schema>'`, then read `.result` from the first line
options.why: The first stream line is the `system/init` event (or a startup event), not the final result. The result comes last.

options.text: `claude -p "..." --append-system-prompt 'Reply only with JSON matching <schema>'`
options.why: Asking for JSON in the prompt is a request, not validation. The output can still drift from the schema.

explanation: If the value is not a valid JSON Schema, `claude` exits with `Error: --json-schema is not a valid JSON Schema`. If the run ends without valid structured output, for example because Claude declined, the response has no `structured_output` field, so check for it before use.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Get structured output)

stem: With `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema '...'`, which top-level field of the JSON response holds the schema-validated object? Type the field name.
explanation: `structured_output` holds the validated object, while `result` still holds Claude's text. The field is missing when the run ended without valid structured output, so a `jq '.structured_output'` step should check that it is present.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Get structured output)

stem: You want a headless run to emit text tokens as they are generated, so a log viewer can show them live. Besides `-p`, which flags does the documented command use? (Choose three.)

options.text: `--output-format stream-json`
options.why: Streaming output is newline-delimited JSON events. The other formats print only at the end.

options.text: `--include-partial-messages`
options.why: Adds `stream_event` partial chunks, including text deltas. It requires `--print` and `stream-json` output.

options.text: `--verbose`
options.why: The documented streaming command passes `--verbose` together with `stream-json` and partial messages.

options.text: `--input-format stream-json`
options.why: Controls how Claude Code reads its input from stdin, not whether the output carries token deltas.

options.text: `--replay-user-messages`
options.why: Echoes user messages from stdin back on stdout. It needs stream-json input and output and has nothing to do with token deltas.

options.text: `--output-format json`
options.why: `json` prints one object when the run ends, so nothing streams.

explanation: The documented pipeline is `claude -p "..." --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages | jq -rj 'select(.type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta") | .event.delta.text'`. The last line of the stream is always the `result` message with the final text, cost and session metadata.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Stream responses)

stem: A nightly job runs `claude -p "Update dependencies and run the tests" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test)"` on Claude Code 2.1.308. No permission mode is set anywhere, there are no hooks and no permission host. Claude decides to run `npm install lodash`. What happens?

options.text: It is denied: the run is in Manual mode, nothing approves the call, and the run continues
options.why: Since v2.1.302, a `-p` run with no mode set starts in Manual (`default`), where a call needing approval is denied unless a rule, hook or prompt tool approves it.

options.text: The run blocks on a permission prompt that nobody can answer, until the CI job's own timeout kills it
options.why: A plain `-p` run has nobody to ask, so requests are denied rather than held. Waiting happens only when a permission host is configured.

options.text: The command runs, because `-p` approves everything that no deny rule blocks
options.why: That describes `bypassPermissions`. Headless runs are not permissive by default.

options.text: Claude Code stops at once with a non-zero exit code and prints no result
options.why: A denial goes back to Claude as a tool result and the run continues. The denial is also listed in the result's `permission_denials`.

explanation: To let the call through, add a rule such as `Bash(npm install *)` or start with `--permission-mode auto` so a classifier reviews actions. Adding `--permission-prompts none` keeps the denials but also tells Claude that nobody can approve, so it does not keep retrying.
reference: Claude Code docs: Choose a permission mode (Tool calls denied in claude -p and Agent SDK runs)

stem: After a cron job ran `claude -p` in a repository, a developer opens a terminal in the same directory and runs `claude --continue` without `-p`. That interactive session picks up the cron job's conversation.

options.text: True
options.why: Interactive `--continue` deliberately skips sessions created with `claude -p` or the Agent SDK.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: those sessions are left out of the picker and out of interactive `--continue`. Use `claude --resume <session-id>`, or `claude -p --continue`, which does include them.

explanation: Claude Code keeps scripted sessions from cluttering a developer's history. They can still be resumed explicitly by ID, and `claude -p --continue` includes `-p`, SDK and `/loop` sessions when it looks for the most recent conversation.
reference: Claude Code docs: Manage sessions (/loop, -p, Agent SDK, and background sessions)

stem: Which statement about `--dangerously-skip-permissions` is accurate?

options.text: It equals `bypassPermissions` mode, yet deny rules still block and it refuses to run as root outside a sandbox
options.why: The CLI reference defines it as equivalent to bypass mode. Deny rules apply in every mode, and the root check is skipped only inside a recognized sandbox.

options.text: It equals `--permission-mode dontAsk`: anything that is not pre-approved is quietly denied
options.why: That is `dontAsk`, the opposite trade-off. Bypass runs nearly everything; `dontAsk` denies whatever is not pre-approved.

options.text: It removes every safeguard at once, deny rules included, so no settings file can block any command Claude chooses to run
options.why: Deny rules block even in bypass mode, and `AskUserQuestion` is one of the actions no mode auto-approves.

options.text: It covers file edits only; shell commands still need their own `--allowedTools` entries
options.why: That is closer to `acceptEdits`. Bypass also covers shell commands, network requests and writes to protected paths.

explanation: The docs recommend bypass mode only for isolated containers or VMs without internet access, because it offers no protection against prompt injection. For a known CI job, `--permission-mode dontAsk` with an exact `--allowedTools` list, or `--permission-mode auto`, is the safer default.
reference: Claude Code docs: Choose a permission mode (Skip all checks with bypassPermissions mode)

stem: A small team wants the Claude Code GitHub Action in one repository to run against a Claude Max subscription rather than API billing. How do they supply the credential?

options.text: Run `claude setup-token` locally, save the token as a `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` secret and pass it to the `claude_code_oauth_token` input
options.why: `setup-token` mints a one-year OAuth token meant for CI and scripts, and the action has a dedicated input for it.

options.text: Copy the logged-in credentials from a developer laptop's Claude config into a repository secret, then restore that file on the runner before the step
options.why: That relies on an interactive login tied to one machine. The documented CI path is the long-lived token from `setup-token`.

options.text: Paste the subscription token into the `anthropic_api_key` input
options.why: An OAuth token is not an API key. Each credential type has its own input.

options.text: Leave auth out, and the action uses the subscription of whoever merged the workflow
options.why: There is no such fallback. The action needs an explicit credential.

explanation: `claude setup-token` prints the token but does not save it, and it needs a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan. For a secret shared across many repositories, the docs prefer a Claude Console API key, because an OAuth token is tied to the subscription of the person who ran `setup-token`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions (Manual setup)

stem: A CI job switches from `claude -p` to `claude --bare -p`. Which statements about its new behaviour are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: A hook in a developer's `~/.claude` settings, or a server in the project's `.mcp.json`, no longer runs
options.why: Bare mode never discovers hooks, plugins or MCP servers, so every machine gets the same run.

options.text: Anthropic API auth must come from `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or from an `apiKeyHelper` passed in `--settings`
options.why: Bare mode never reads OAuth credentials or the keychain.

options.text: The project's `CLAUDE.md` still loads, because it lives in the repository rather than in user config
options.why: CLAUDE.md auto-discovery is skipped too. Pass rules explicitly, for example with `--append-system-prompt-file`.

options.text: Claude has no tools at all, so the job can only produce text
options.why: The Bash, file read and file edit tools stay available.

options.text: A command that hits its timeout moves to the background, as in a normal session
options.why: No background tasks run in bare mode. A command that reaches its timeout stops instead.

explanation: `--bare` is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and is planned to become the default for `-p`. Context you still need goes in with flags: `--append-system-prompt(-file)`, `--settings`, `--mcp-config`, `--agents` and `--plugin-dir`. Bare mode also drops system reminders, so Claude is not told when a file it read changes on disk.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Start faster with bare mode)

stem: A GitHub Actions step runs `claude --bare -p "..."` with `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` set from a token generated by `claude setup-token` last week. The step fails to authenticate, yet the same token works when `--bare` is removed. What is the cause?

options.text: Bare mode never reads OAuth credentials, `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` included; use `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or an `apiKeyHelper` in `--settings`
options.why: The authentication docs state it directly: bare mode does not read `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.

options.text: Tokens from `setup-token` expire after seven days and must be generated again
options.why: `setup-token` creates a one-year token, and the same token works without `--bare`.

options.text: Bare mode ignores the process environment entirely, so even `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` has to be passed inside the `--settings` JSON instead
options.why: Bare mode does read `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment. Only the OAuth and keychain sources are excluded.

options.text: Tokens from `setup-token` only work in interactive sessions
options.why: They are made for CI and scripts. The failure here is specific to bare mode.

explanation: Bare mode narrows auth on purpose so a run never picks up a stray login from the machine. On Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry, bare mode keeps reading that provider's own credentials as usual.
reference: Claude Code docs: Authentication (Generate a long-lived token)

stem: Put the manual setup of the Claude Code GitHub Action (without running `/install-github-app`) in order.

options.text: Install the Claude GitHub App on the repository
Add `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`) as a repository secret
Copy `examples/claude.yml` into `.github/workflows/`
Mention `@claude` in an issue or pull request comment to test it

explanation: You need admin access to the repository. The app supplies the Contents, Issues and Pull requests write access the action relies on; the workflow file references the secret by name, so the secret must exist before the first run; and a mention is the quickest test of interactive mode. `/install-github-app` automates the same steps for github.com repositories.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions (Manual setup)

stem: Which statement about Claude Code for GitLab CI/CD is accurate?

options.text: A GitLab-maintained beta: your job installs the CLI on your runner and runs `claude -p`, with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in a masked variable
options.why: The docs describe exactly this: a `.gitlab-ci.yml` job that installs Claude Code and calls it, with the key in a masked CI/CD variable.

options.text: It reuses `anthropics/claude-code-action`, which GitLab runners can execute natively
options.why: That is a GitHub Action. The GitLab path is an ordinary pipeline job that calls the CLI.

options.text: `/install-github-app` detects a gitlab.com remote and configures the pipeline for you
options.why: The command only works with github.com repositories; on a gitlab.com remote it prints a notice and exits.

options.text: Jobs run on Anthropic-hosted runners that GitLab provisions on demand, so the pipeline needs no image, no CLI install and no stored key
options.why: Jobs run on your own GitLab runners, under your branch protection and approvals.

explanation: The example job uses `--permission-mode acceptEdits` with an explicit `--allowedTools` list. For Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform, the job exchanges GitLab's OIDC token for cloud credentials, so no static keys are stored. Mention-driven runs need your own webhook listener that calls the pipeline trigger API with variables such as `AI_FLOW_INPUT`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitLab CI/CD

stem: A job runs `claude -p ... --mcp-config approvals.json --permission-prompt-tool mcp__approvals__ask`, where the tool posts each permission request to Slack and waits for a reply. That suits daytime runs, but the same job also runs overnight when nobody answers, and those runs hang. What change makes the overnight runs finish without weakening the permission checks?

options.text: Add `--permission-prompts none` to the overnight invocation
options.why: Requests that nothing else resolves are then denied instead of sent to the tool, Claude is told nobody can approve them, and `AskUserQuestion` is removed. Rules, hooks and the mode still decide everything first.

options.text: Run the overnight job with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` so no prompt is ever raised
options.why: The run would finish, but only by removing the checks, which breaks the requirement.

options.text: Add `--max-turns 20` so the run stops after a bounded number of turns
options.why: A turn that is waiting on a permission answer never completes, so a turn cap does not end the wait.

options.text: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS` to a few minutes
options.why: That caps idle waiting for background work after the final turn. A pending permission request is a different kind of wait.

explanation: Without the flag, a run that has a permission host (a `--permission-prompt-tool` or an SDK `canUseTool` callback) waits for that host to answer each request. `--permission-prompts none` (Claude Code 2.1.259 or later) makes the unattended variant explicit. With `stream-json` output the denials appear as `permission_denied` system messages and in the result's `permission_denials`, so the morning review can see what was blocked.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Turn off permission prompts in unattended runs)

stem: Which statements about `claude -p --permission-prompts none` are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: Permission rules, `PermissionRequest` hooks and the permission mode still decide each call first; only requests nothing else resolves are denied
options.why: The flag only replaces the missing human answer. It does not override the rest of the permission flow.

options.text: Tools that need a person's answer, such as `AskUserQuestion`, are removed so Claude cannot call them
options.why: The docs state this directly. MCP elicitation requests that no `Elicitation` hook answers are cancelled as well.

options.text: With `stream-json` output, denials appear as `permission_denied` system messages and in the result's `permission_denials`
options.why: This lets a scheduled job report what it was not allowed to do.

options.text: It denies every tool call, including calls that `--allowedTools` entries match
options.why: Allowed calls still run. Only calls that would otherwise prompt are denied.

options.text: It makes the run exit with a non-zero code at the first denied call
options.why: Claude is told that nobody can approve the request and not to retry it, and the run continues.

options.text: It is another spelling of `--permission-mode dontAsk`, so the two cannot be combined
options.why: It sets who answers prompts, not the mode, and combines with any mode, for example `--permission-mode auto --permission-prompts none`.

explanation: The default value, `host`, sends prompts to the Agent SDK host or the `--permission-prompt-tool`. The value `none` says nobody is there. In a `-p` run with no host the requests are denied either way, but the flag also stops Claude from retrying them and removes question-asking tools.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Turn off permission prompts in unattended runs)

stem: A pull request adds a workflow that runs `claude -p "Review this PR and fix what you find" --dangerously-skip-permissions` on a GitHub-hosted runner with repository secrets in the environment and open internet access. Which review objection is accurate?

options.text: Bypass mode gives no protection against prompt injection, so text planted in the diff could get Claude to send secrets out
options.why: The docs warn that bypass mode offers no protection against prompt injection and recommend it only for isolated environments without internet access.

options.text: The flag is ignored in `-p` mode, so the job will just stall on permission prompts
options.why: The flag works with `-p`, and in non-interactive mode no warning dialog is shown.

options.text: Bypass mode also switches off deny rules, so the repository's `Bash(curl *)` deny rule no longer stops Claude from posting data anywhere
options.why: Deny rules block in every mode, bypass included. The real weakness is that a deny list rarely covers every exfiltration route.

options.text: GitHub-hosted runners run jobs as root, so Claude Code silently falls back to Manual mode
options.why: When Claude Code refuses to bypass as root it fails to start with an error. It does not switch modes quietly.

explanation: PR content is untrusted input. For a known job, prefer `--permission-mode dontAsk` with an exact `--allowedTools` list, or auto mode, where a classifier reviews actions. Keep bypass mode for disposable containers with no secrets and no network.
reference: Claude Code docs: Choose a permission mode (Skip all checks with bypassPermissions mode)

stem: A `claude -p` CI step prints its final result, but the process keeps running until the job's 60-minute timeout. The transcript shows Claude started `npm run dev` as a background Bash command to check a page. Which explanation and fix are right?

options.text: It waits for that command to exit or time out, ignoring the 10-minute cap; `--bare` runs start no background tasks
options.why: For a background command the main conversation started, the run waits until it exits or reaches its time limit. In bare mode no background tasks run, so a command that times out stops instead.

options.text: Claude Code is waiting for the CI runner to finish draining stdout; redirecting the output to a file lets the process exit
options.why: The wait for a slow reader is capped at 30 seconds, so it cannot explain an hour.

options.text: `CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS` is set too high; lowering it to 60000 ends the wait
options.why: That ceiling does not end the wait while a background command started by the main conversation is still running.

options.text: Session persistence keeps the process alive to flush the transcript; add `--no-session-persistence`
options.why: Skipping the transcript has nothing to do with waiting for background work.

explanation: After its turn ends and stdin closes, a `-p` run also stays open for background subagents and workflows, Monitor watches and pending `/loop` wakeups. A `--max-budget-usd` cap that is reached stops remaining background work instead of waiting. When stderr is a terminal, Claude Code prints `Waiting for background work to finish` after five seconds, naming the work.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Background tasks at exit)

stem: A process supervisor stops long `claude -p` runs during deploys. When engineers later resume those sessions, the interrupted turn has no result recorded. They want the in-progress turn to end properly before the process goes away. What should the supervisor do?

options.text: Send SIGINT (or call the Agent SDK's `interrupt()`) to end the turn first, then stop the process
options.why: The docs say to send SIGINT or call `interrupt()` before stopping the process if you want the turn ended rather than left unfinished.

options.text: Keep sending SIGTERM, because Claude Code always finishes the turn in progress before it exits on that signal
options.why: On SIGTERM, Claude Code leaves the turn unfinished, records no result for it and exits with code 143.

options.text: Send SIGKILL, so the transcript is never left half-written
options.why: SIGKILL gives Claude Code no chance to clean up: no killing of Bash process trees and no `SessionEnd` hooks.

options.text: Close stdin and wait, because a `-p` run treats end of input as an order to finish the turn
options.why: End of input does not end a model turn. A text-mode run has usually closed stdin already.

explanation: On SIGTERM, Claude Code terminates the process tree of any running Bash command, records it as killed, runs `SessionEnd` hooks and exits with 143, starting no new tool call or model request. On resume, the interrupted turn stays as it is unless `CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN=1` asks Claude to continue it.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Stop a run with SIGTERM)

stem: Job A in a GitHub workflow runs `claude -p ... --output-format json` and saves `session_id` as a job output. Job B, on a fresh runner, runs `claude -p "Apply the fixes" --resume "$ID"` and cannot find the conversation. What is the right fix?

options.text: Carry Job A's `.jsonl` transcript over as an artifact and pass its absolute path to `--resume`
options.why: Sessions are transcript files on the machine that ran them. `--resume` accepts a transcript's absolute path in place of an ID.

options.text: Add `--fork-session`, which downloads the session from Anthropic by its ID
options.why: Sessions are stored locally. `--fork-session` only gives a resumed conversation a new ID.

options.text: Use `--continue` instead, which searches every project on the machine
options.why: `--continue` picks the most recent conversation in the current directory, and a fresh runner has none.

options.text: Pass `--session-id "$ID"` in Job B, which tells Claude Code to reattach to the existing conversation with that UUID
options.why: `--session-id` sets the UUID of the conversation you are starting. It does not import a transcript from another machine.

explanation: Claude Code searches for a session ID across every project, but only on the current machine. Job A also must not use `--no-session-persistence`, or there is no transcript to carry over. Transcripts can contain secrets from tool output, so treat the artifact accordingly.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Continue conversations)

stem: Which statements about the turn and cost caps in `claude -p` are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: `--max-turns` has no limit by default and makes the run exit with an error when the limit is reached
options.why: This is how the CLI reference describes the flag.

options.text: Once spend reaches `--max-budget-usd`, Claude Code stops background work that is still running instead of waiting for it
options.why: A reached cap ends background subagents, and spawning another subagent fails with `Budget limit reached`.

options.text: `--max-budget-usd` is checked against the amount on your Anthropic invoice
options.why: It is checked against Claude Code's client-side cost estimate, which can differ from the bill.

options.text: Spend by subagents is tracked separately and does not count toward `--max-budget-usd`
options.why: Subagent spend counts toward the cap.

options.text: Both caps also apply to interactive sessions started without `-p`
options.why: Both flags are print mode only.

explanation: Use both caps together: turns bound the length of the loop and the budget bounds money. When you return to a conversation with `--continue` or `--resume`, totals restored from earlier runs do not count toward the new cap, even though the JSON `total_cost_usd` reports the conversation's whole total.
reference: Claude Code docs: CLI reference (CLI flags)

stem: A wrapper script runs plain `claude -p`, not through an SDK, and wants a person on Slack to approve or reject each permission request as it happens. Which mechanism is designed for that?

options.text: An MCP tool that asks on Slack, loaded with `--mcp-config` and named in `--permission-prompt-tool`
options.why: `--permission-prompt-tool mcp__<server>__<tool>` is the CLI's way to hand permission prompts to an MCP tool in non-interactive mode; the tool can ask Slack and return the decision.

options.text: `--input-format stream-json`, writing `yes` or `no` to stdin as user messages when a request appears
options.why: A user message is new conversational input, not an answer to a pending permission request.

options.text: `--permission-prompts host` on its own, which shows requests in the terminal that launched the job
options.why: `host` is the default and means an SDK host or prompt tool answers. With neither configured, requests are simply denied.

options.text: `--replay-user-messages`, which pauses the run until stdin echoes back an approval
options.why: It only re-emits stdin user messages on stdout as an acknowledgement.

explanation: Claude Code waits for the prompt tool's MCP server to connect before the first turn, up to `MCP_TIMEOUT` (30 seconds by default). The prompt tool cannot approve an MCP tool marked as requiring user interaction: an `allow` for one is turned into a deny. An application built on the Agent SDK uses a `canUseTool` callback for the same job.
reference: Claude Code docs: CLI reference (--permission-prompt-tool)

stem: A host process keeps one `claude -p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --verbose` process open and writes the person's follow-up messages to its stdin. What should each input line look like?

options.text: One JSON object per line, such as `{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":"Use Postgres"}}`
options.why: Streaming input takes SDK user messages: `type: "user"` with a Messages API user message in `message`.

options.text: The plain text of the message followed by a newline, exactly as in text mode
options.why: That is `--input-format text`. `stream-json` expects newline-delimited JSON messages.

options.text: A bare Messages API message on each line, such as `{"role":"user","content":"Use Postgres"}`, with no envelope
options.why: That object belongs inside the `message` field of an envelope whose `type` is `"user"`; on its own it is not an SDK user message.

options.text: `{"type":"prompt","text":"Use Postgres"}`, mirroring the events in the output stream
options.why: Input lines use the SDK user message shape, with `type: "user"` and a `message` field, not a `prompt` type with a `text` field.

explanation: This is the same shape the Agent SDK's streaming-input examples yield. `content` can be a string or an array of content blocks such as text and images. A message that is still queued when `--max-turns` ends a turn stays queued and starts a new turn with its own limit. Add `--replay-user-messages` if the host wants each input echoed back on stdout as an acknowledgement.
reference: Agent SDK docs: Handle approvals and user input; TypeScript SDK reference (SDKUserMessage)

stem: In a CI run with `--permission-mode dontAsk`, adding `AskUserQuestion` to `--allowedTools` lets Claude ask the user clarifying questions.

options.text: True
options.why: `dontAsk` denies `AskUserQuestion` even when an allow rule matches it.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `dontAsk` never collects answers, so it denies `AskUserQuestion` whatever the allow rules say. Claude has to proceed on its own judgment.

explanation: `AskUserQuestion` is one of the actions no permission mode auto-approves, because it needs a person. In `dontAsk` it is denied outright, together with explicit `ask` rules and MCP tools marked as requiring user interaction. If a pipeline really needs a person's input, use a permission host such as an SDK `canUseTool` callback, or defer the call and resume later.
reference: Claude Code docs: Choose a permission mode (Allow only pre-approved tools with dontAsk mode)

stem: Which statements about how `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` decides what to do are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: When the workflow sets a `prompt` input, the action runs in automation mode without waiting for an `@claude` mention, and results go to the workflow log by default
options.why: This is automation mode. Claude posts to the issue or PR only if the prompt tells it to and it has a tool that can post.

options.text: On a schedule with a plain-text prompt, Claude has no shell or GitHub API access until you grant tools through `claude_args` or a `permissions.allow` rule in `settings`
options.why: Scheduled automation starts locked down. A skill prompt can instead rely on its own `allowed-tools` frontmatter.

options.text: Automation mode skips the actor checks, so bot accounts can start runs freely
options.why: The human-actor check runs on every event. A bot has to be listed in `allowed_bots`.

options.text: Without a `prompt` input, the action reviews every pull request event automatically
options.why: Without a prompt it runs in interactive mode and waits for the trigger phrase.

options.text: You must set `mode: automation` to switch from interactive mode
options.why: v1 detects the mode itself. The `mode` input was removed in the upgrade from beta.

explanation: Mode follows from the presence of `prompt`. In both modes the action checks the triggering actor before Claude starts: write access on issue and PR events (unless `allowed_non_write_users` is set together with your own `github_token`), and a human, non-bot actor on every event.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions (Interactive and automation modes)

stem: Match each Claude Code GitHub Action symptom with its documented cause.

options.text: The workflow passes `github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` to the action
options.why: Commits made with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger workflows.

options.text: The commenter does not have write access to the repository
options.why: The write-access check rejects them unless allowed_non_write_users is set.

options.text: The cron schedule was last edited by a bot account
options.why: Scheduled runs are attributed to that user, and bots must be listed in allowed_bots.

options.text: GitHub withholds secrets from fork pull requests on public repositories
options.why: So a secret-based review cannot authenticate on fork PRs.

prompts.text: Claude pushes commits to a PR, but the repository's CI never runs on them
An outside contributor writes `@claude fix this` on an issue and the run fails before Claude starts
A daily scheduled report fails the actor check every morning
The review workflow works for branches in the repository but never for PRs from forks

explanation: Remove the `github_token` input so the action authenticates as the Claude GitHub App, or pass a custom app token. Set `allowed_non_write_users` (with your own `github_token`) for trusted non-writers, list automation accounts in `allowed_bots`, and expect fork PRs on public repositories to get no secrets.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions (Troubleshooting; Who can trigger runs)

stem: A repository commits `.claude/settings.json` with `"permissions": {"allow": ["Bash(npm test)"]}`. On a developer laptop that has trusted the folder, `claude -p "run the tests"` runs `npm test`. In CI on a fresh checkout, the same command is denied and stderr warns that the workspace has not been trusted. Which fix is correct?

options.text: Pass the rule on the command line with `--allowedTools "Bash(npm test)"`
options.why: A `-p` run never shows the trust dialog, and project `permissions.allow` rules stay unused in a folder that was never trusted. A rule passed on the command line comes from you, not from the repository.

options.text: Add `--setting-sources project` so that Claude Code reads the project settings file
options.why: Choosing setting sources does not trust the folder, and untrusted project allow rules stay unused.

options.text: Run with `--bare` so that the workspace trust check is skipped
options.why: Bare mode cuts down what is discovered from the project. It does not make untrusted project allow rules apply.

options.text: Switch to `--permission-mode acceptEdits`, which also approves test commands
options.why: `acceptEdits` approves file edits and common filesystem commands such as `mkdir` and `mv`. `npm test` still needs an allow rule.

explanation: The trust rules are asymmetric. In a never-trusted folder, a `-p` run still uses the repository's hooks and its `env` block, but not its `permissions.allow` rules or `additionalDirectories`. You can also mark the folder trusted with `projects["<path>"].hasTrustDialogAccepted` in `~/.claude.json`, but an explicit `--allowedTools` keeps the CI job self-describing.
reference: Claude Code docs: Configure permissions (What runs before you trust a folder)

stem: A CI runner has several Claude credentials set at the same time. Order them from the one Claude Code uses first to the one it uses last.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock credentials, with `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1` set
`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
The output of an `apiKeyHelper` script
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`

explanation: Selecting a cloud provider wins, then the bearer token used for LLM gateways, then the API key, then the helper script, then the long-lived OAuth token from `claude setup-token`. Anthropic profiles and the `/login` subscription come after these. In `-p` mode an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is always used when present, without the one-time approval interactive sessions ask for, so a stale key left on a runner can quietly win over the credential you meant to use.
reference: Claude Code docs: Authentication (Authentication precedence)

stem: A product lets users start agent tasks from a web app. Claude sometimes calls `AskUserQuestion`, and users may answer hours later. Workers are recycled every 15 minutes, so no process may wait that long. Which design fits?

options.text: A `PreToolUse` hook that defers `AskUserQuestion`; resume the session once the user answers
options.why: The docs recommend the `defer` decision when a user may take longer than the process can stay running: the run ends, the app stores the question, and a later `claude -p --resume` supplies the answer through the hook.

options.text: A `canUseTool` callback that awaits the user's answer, since the callback may stay pending indefinitely
options.why: It may, but only while the process lives. Recycling the worker kills the pending callback and the run with it.

options.text: Run with `--permission-prompts none` and let Claude choose sensible defaults instead of asking
options.why: That removes `AskUserQuestion` altogether, so the user is never asked.

options.text: Set `askUserQuestionTimeout` to `10m` so unanswered questions auto-continue before the recycle
options.why: That setting closes the question and lets Claude proceed without the answer. It does not deliver an answer that arrives later.

explanation: Pick the waiting strategy by how long a person might take. If the answer comes back within the life of the process, a `canUseTool` callback that awaits it is simplest. If it can take longer than a worker lives, defer: the pending call stays in the persisted session, and a later `claude -p --resume` hands the answer back through the hook.
reference: Agent SDK docs: Handle approvals and user input

stem: An Agent SDK app relays Claude's clarifying questions to its user through `canUseTool`. Put one round trip in order.

options.text: Claude calls `AskUserQuestion` with a `questions` array of multiple-choice questions
The `canUseTool` callback fires with the tool name `AskUserQuestion`
The app shows each question and its options and collects the labels the user picks
The callback returns `allow` with `updatedInput` holding the original `questions` and an `answers` map from question text to label
Claude continues the task using the answers

explanation: Each call carries 1 to 4 questions with 2 to 4 options each. For a multi-select question, pass an array of labels; for free text, put the user's own words in place of a label. If you restrict tools with a `tools` list, include `AskUserQuestion`, and remember it is not available inside subagents spawned through the Agent tool.
reference: Agent SDK docs: Handle approvals and user input (Handle clarifying questions)

stem: A team builds a terminal front end over `claude -p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --verbose` and wants Claude's clarifying questions answered by the person at the keyboard. Which statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: A user message written to stdin is new conversational input; the answer to a pending `AskUserQuestion` call has to return through the permission flow, as `updatedInput` with the answers
options.why: Clarifying questions arrive as a tool call routed to the permission host, and the answers go back as the tool's input when the call is allowed.

options.text: Adding `--permission-prompts none` removes `AskUserQuestion`, so Claude cannot ask anything in that run
options.why: Tools that need a person's answer are removed when nobody is declared to answer prompts.

options.text: `--replay-user-messages` makes Claude pause after each question until the person replies
options.why: It only echoes user messages from stdin back on stdout.

options.text: Subagents spawned through the Agent tool can put questions to the person directly with `AskUserQuestion`
options.why: `AskUserQuestion` is not currently available in subagents spawned through the Agent tool.

options.text: If the person never answers, Claude Code auto-continues after 60 seconds by default
options.why: By default questions wait for an answer. The auto-continue timeout is an opt-in setting.

explanation: Two channels are easy to confuse. Stdin user messages steer the conversation: new instructions, extra context, follow-ups. Approvals and question answers travel through the permission host, which is the SDK's `canUseTool` (carried over the same stdio connection as control requests) or a `--permission-prompt-tool`. A front end that pipes the person's reply into stdin as chat leaves the tool call unanswered.
reference: Agent SDK docs: Handle approvals and user input

stem: A company runs 30 headless `claude -p` workers on shared servers for its customer-facing code-review product. They all use one engineer's subscription login, copied to each server, and runs fail intermittently with login-expired errors. Which credential approach should they move to?

options.text: A Claude Console API key in `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or one fetched by an `apiKeyHelper` from a vault
options.why: An API key is a static credential with nothing to refresh, and third-party products must use API key auth rather than claude.ai login.

options.text: A `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` generated once with `claude setup-token` and handed to every worker through its environment
options.why: It lasts a year and suits personal scripts, but it is still one person's subscription behind a product sold to customers.

options.text: Have each worker run `/login` when it starts
options.why: `/login` is a terminal-interface command that is not available in `-p`, and it is still subscription OAuth.

options.text: Keep the shared login and add a cron job that copies a fresh credentials file every hour
options.why: It keeps one person's subscription login behind a customer-facing product and still depends on refreshing an OAuth login.

explanation: Unless Anthropic has approved it, third-party developers may not offer claude.ai login or subscription rate limits in their products, including agents built on the Agent SDK. An OAuth login refreshes itself and fails when it cannot, while a static key or a vault-backed `apiKeyHelper` behaves predictably across many concurrent processes.
reference: Agent SDK docs: Agent SDK overview; Claude Code docs: Authentication

stem: Security has banned long-lived AI credentials in GitHub secrets. The Claude Code GitHub Action must call the Claude API directly, not Bedrock or Vertex, across 40 repositories. Which setup satisfies this?

options.text: Workload identity federation with `anthropic_federation_rule_id`, `anthropic_organization_id` and `id-token: write`
options.why: The action exchanges the workflow's GitHub OIDC token for Claude API access through a Console service account, so no long-lived secret is stored.

options.text: One organization-level `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` secret, because an OAuth token is not a static API key and so does not count as long-lived
options.why: It is still a stored one-year credential, and it is tied to the subscription of whoever generated it.

options.text: An organization-level `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret that is rotated every quarter
options.why: Rotation shortens exposure, but the key is still a long-lived stored secret.

options.text: Set `use_bedrock: "true"` with OIDC and keep the Claude API as the provider
options.why: That routes inference through Amazon Bedrock, which the requirement rules out.

explanation: `anthropic_service_account_id` and `anthropic_workspace_id` are optional when the federation rule already targets them. The workflow needs `id-token: write` for the exchange even if you pass your own `github_token`. Bedrock, Agent Platform and Foundry also use OIDC federation, but each through its own provider.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions (Set up for an organization)

stem: A code-scanning service runs `claude --bare -p` against customer repositories it has never seen, assuming nothing in a repository's `.claude/settings.json` can affect the run. Which part of that file still applies under `--bare`?

options.text: The `env` block, along with helper commands such as `awsAuthRefresh`
options.why: The docs note that under `--bare` the project's `env` block and helpers such as `awsAuthRefresh` still apply.

options.text: The `hooks` it defines, because bare mode only skips hooks from user-level settings
options.why: Bare mode skips hooks from settings files and from installed plugins.

options.text: Its `permissions.allow` rules
options.why: In a folder that was never trusted, a `-p` run does not use project allow rules at all.

options.text: Its `apiKeyHelper` setting
options.why: Under bare mode, Claude Code reads `apiKeyHelper` only from `--settings`.

explanation: An `env` block can redirect proxies, endpoints or tool behaviour, so it is not harmless. To keep a repository's settings out completely, also pass `--setting-sources user`, so Claude Code reads neither the project's settings files nor its `.mcp.json`. Run untrusted repositories in a sandbox or container as well.
reference: Claude Code docs: Configure permissions (What runs before you trust a folder)

stem: A pipeline runs `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema '...'` with a schema whose `email` property has `"format": "email"`, then inserts `.structured_output.email` into a CRM. Two problems appear: a few records hold strings that are not email addresses, and now and then the insert step crashes on a missing field. What is the right fix?

options.text: Check that `structured_output` exists before using it, and validate the email format in your own code
options.why: Claude Code treats `format` as an annotation and does not enforce it, and a run that ends without valid structured output has no `structured_output` field.

options.text: Claude Code rejects schemas containing `format` at startup, so the job must be running an older schema; redeploy it
options.why: Schemas that use `format` are accepted; the keyword simply is not enforced.

options.text: Switch to `--output-format stream-json`, where structured output is validated more strictly
options.why: The output format does not change how the schema is validated.

options.text: Add a `pattern` to the schema and drop the presence check, since a valid schema guarantees the field
options.why: No schema guarantees the field: if Claude declines the request, the response has no `structured_output` at all.

explanation: Treat headless structured output as you would any external input: check that it is present, then validate whatever the schema validator does not enforce. A missing field usually means the run ended without valid output, so look at `is_error` and the result before retrying blindly.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Get structured output)

stem: Your wrapper uses exit codes to tell a supervisor shutdown apart from a failed run. When a running `claude -p` process is stopped with SIGTERM, which exit code does Claude Code return? Type the number.
explanation: 143 follows the usual 128 + signal-number convention (SIGTERM is 15). A failed run returns some other non-zero code and prints the failure as its result on stdout, while an invalid flag is reported on stderr before the run starts. After a SIGTERM the interrupted turn has no recorded result.
reference: Claude Code docs: Run Claude Code programmatically (Stop a run with SIGTERM)

stem: Match each `claude -p` scenario with the permission mode that fits it best.

options.text: `dontAsk`
options.why: Denies anything that would prompt; only pre-approved actions and those needing no approval run.

options.text: `auto`
options.why: A classifier reviews actions instead of a person.

options.text: `acceptEdits`
options.why: File edits and common filesystem commands run without prompting.

options.text: `bypassPermissions`
options.why: Skips permission checks; meant for isolated environments only.

prompts.text: A CI job that may only read files and run exactly `npm test`
A long unattended task where you want a safety review without listing every command in advance
Applying lint fixes to files, with nothing else expected
A throwaway container with no internet and no secrets, running fully autonomously

explanation: The docs' CI recipe is `--permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Bash(npm test)" "Read"`. Auto mode needs a supported model and can be turned off by your organization. `acceptEdits` still needs allow rules for other shell commands. Bypass mode belongs only inside a container or VM, and only as a non-root user on Linux and macOS.
reference: Claude Code docs: Choose a permission mode (Common setups)

stem: A review workflow installs the `code-review` plugin and sets `prompt: "/code-review:code-review --comment ..."`. The skill's own `allowed-tools` frontmatter lists `mcp__github_inline_comment__create_inline_comment`, so the author deleted the `claude_args` line that named the same tool. Now reviews appear only in the run log. Why?

options.text: The action starts the inline-comment MCP server only when `claude_args` names the tool in `--allowedTools`
options.why: The docs say to keep the `claude_args` line for exactly this reason, even though the skill's frontmatter names the same tool.

options.text: Without `claude_args`, the action drops back to interactive mode and waits for an `@claude` mention
options.why: The mode depends on the `prompt` input, which is still set.

options.text: `--comment` needs `pull-requests: write` on the job, and the example grants only read access
options.why: The documented review example posts comments with `pull-requests: read`. The comments go through the MCP tool.

options.text: Skills that come from plugins cannot pre-approve tools, so the `allowed-tools` frontmatter is ignored when the action runs in CI
options.why: Skills can pre-approve tools with `allowed-tools`. The problem is that the server providing the tool never started.

explanation: Pre-approving a tool and having it exist are different things. A permission entry only helps once a server provides the tool, and here it is the action's `--allowedTools` scan that decides whether the inline-comment server starts. When a tool seems to be ignored, check the `system/init` tool list before you touch permissions.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions (Run a skill)

stem: A PR-triggered Claude workflow sometimes runs for an hour, and on busy days several runs pile up. Which changes follow the documented guidance for bounding cost? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add `--max-turns` to `claude_args` and set a workflow-level timeout
options.why: Both appear in the docs' cost guidance: one bounds the loop, the other bounds wall-clock time and runner minutes.

options.text: Use GitHub's concurrency controls to limit parallel runs
options.why: The docs list concurrency controls for limiting parallel runs, which stops runs piling up.

options.text: Set the `max_turns` input on the action step
options.why: That is a beta-era input. In v1, CLI options go in `claude_args`.

options.text: Switch to an organization-wide `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` so that runs stop costing anything
options.why: Runs would draw on one person's subscription instead of API billing, and they still use Actions minutes.

options.text: Pass `github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` so the action skips the GitHub App and runs faster
options.why: This has nothing to do with cost, and commits made with GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger CI workflows.

explanation: Each run costs GitHub Actions minutes as well as tokens. Besides hard caps, the docs suggest specific `@claude` requests, issue templates that give context up front, and a concise `CLAUDE.md`, which is read on every run. A raw `claude -p` job can also add `--max-budget-usd`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions (Manage costs)

stem: Step 1 runs `claude -p "Refactor utils" --permission-mode acceptEdits --output-format json`. Step 2 runs `claude -p "Also update the callers" --resume "$ID"`. In step 2, Claude's file edits are denied. Why?

options.text: `-p --resume` starts in the mode a new `-p` run would use, not the session's earlier mode
options.why: Non-interactive resumes do not restore the stored permission mode (plan mode is the only, conditional, exception), so pass `--permission-mode acceptEdits` again.

options.text: Resumed sessions are read-only until you add `--fork-session`
options.why: There is no read-only rule. `--fork-session` only gives the resumed conversation a new ID.

options.text: `acceptEdits` approvals are stored per session ID, and `--resume` assigns a new ID
options.why: `--resume` keeps the original ID unless you also pass `--fork-session`.

options.text: Files edited in step 1 became protected paths, and `acceptEdits` never auto-approves a second edit to a protected path
options.why: Protected paths are a fixed set of sensitive locations. Editing a file does not add it to that set.

explanation: Treat every `claude -p` invocation as standalone configuration: repeat the permission flags, allowed tools and budget on each step. A session that ended in plan mode resumes in plan mode with `-p` only when you pass `--permission-prompt-tool` (without `--permission-prompts none`) and no `--permission-mode` or `--fork-session`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Manage sessions (Permission mode on resume)
